item.text: {"question_id":"3B.6","answer":"During López Obrador’s 2018–2023 period, Mexico showed a mixed and uncertain safety outcome rather than a clear lawful reduction in exposure-adjusted violence. Positive indicators include a 17.3% comparison-point decline in homicide deaths, a 12% fall in reported crime per 100,000 inhabitants from 2018 to 2023, declines in street robbery, extortion, vehicle theft, and household robbery, and a 5.3% homicide-rate decline with a fourth consecutive annual improvement in peacefulness in 2023 (BATCH-0016-E009; BATCH-0004-E019). Earlier victimization and insecurity measures also declined, although the main survey evidence predates 2023 (BATCH-0021-R01-E012). These gains were not clearly attributable to the federal strategy: the National Guard’s expansion did not consistently correspond to subnational homicide reductions, and a comparative analysis found that the absence of National Guard operations was the configuration associated with homicide reduction (BATCH-0016-E008; BATCH-0016-E011). The positive trend also deteriorated in the target year: reported crime rose 15.9% from 2022 to 2023; lesions, threats, fraud, and several other offenses increased; more than 30,500 people were killed; organized-crime violence remained severe; political killings reached a record; and peace remained 14.4% worse than in 2015 (BATCH-0016-E009; BATCH-0004-E019). Interpretation is further limited by high cifra negra, possible undercounting or reclassification of homicides, increased reported disappearances despite declining homicide, and the absence of a complete exposure-adjusted national violence series (BATCH-0021-R01-E012; BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0016-E009). The means were not consistently lawful or proportionate: the UN Working Group linked frequent military policing to violence, torture, disappearances, and homicides and found arbitrary detention widespread; Mexico Evalúa documented serious military-execution allegations and persistent impunity; and reporting described apparent civilian shootings in Nuevo Laredo, though the factual and presidential attribution remain contested (BATCH-0049-E011; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0010-E004). Thus, the evidence supports some real aggregate safety improvements, but not a demonstrated exposure-adjusted reduction achieved through demonstrably lawful, proportionate policy without a broader fear or abuse climate. Organized crime, inherited institutional weakness, local responsibility, measurement changes, and external firearms supply constrain causal attribution to López Obrador (BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0016-E011).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0016-E009","BATCH-0004-E019","BATCH-0021-R01-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E003","BATCH-0016-E008","BATCH-0016-E011","BATCH-0051-E017","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0016-E005","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0047-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence does not provide a complete exposure-adjusted national series covering criminal, communal, and insurgent violence for the full period.","High cifra negra, reporting changes, possible homicide undercounting or reclassification, and rising disappearance reports weaken direct interpretation of aggregate declines.","Several positive indicators are national or subnational outcomes without causal identification of López Obrador’s contribution; local institutions performed most routine security activity.","The supplied military-abuse evidence establishes serious allegations, investigations, and systemic risks but does not establish direct presidential orders for individual incidents.","The evidence does not definitively establish a nationwide broader fear climate, although persistent organized-crime violence, political killings, disappearances, arbitrary detention, and abuse materially qualify the safety gains."],"corrections_made":["Recast the outcome as mixed rather than describing the positive reductions chiefly as modest and contested.","Incorporated the documented 2018–2023 declines across multiple crime categories while preserving the 2022–2023 deterioration.","Added reporting-freedom and underreporting limitations, including high cifra negra and increased disappearances despite declining homicide.","Separated aggregate safety outcomes from evidence about whether the militarized federal strategy caused them.","Preserved the lawful-and-proportionate-policy test by explicitly weighing arbitrary detention, torture, alleged extrajudicial killings, impunity, and weak accountability.","Kept the target period centered on 2018–2023 and retained causal limits from inherited conditions, local responsibility, measurement changes, organized crime, and external firearms supply."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A fuller exposure-adjusted violence series could change the balance between genuine safety improvement and measurement artifact.","Additional target-period evidence on communal violence, insurgent violence, reporting suppression, and population-level fear could materially refine the conclusion.","Final assessment would benefit from independently verified evidence on remedies, prosecutions, and civilian oversight for military and National Guard abuses."]}
